message.content:
**ATP synthase (also called F₁F₀‑ATPase) – the “molecular motor” of mitochondria** | Feature | What it does | |---------|--------------| | **Location** | Embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IM). | | **Structure** | Two main parts: the membrane‑embedded **F₀** sector (proton channel) and the soluble **F₁** sector (catalytic core). | | **Energy source** | Uses the proton motive force (ΔpH + ΔΨ) generated by the electron transport chain (ETC). | | **Catalytic reaction** | **ADP + Pi + H⁺ (in the matrix) → ATP + H₂O** (hydrolysis of inorganic phosphate). | | **Mechanism** | 1. Protons flow back into the matrix through F₀, causing rotation of the c‑ring. 2. Rotation drives conformational changes in the F₁ β‑subunits, cycling them through loose, tight, and open states that bind ADP/Pi, synthesize ATP, and release it. | | **Directionality** | In normal respiration, it works **forward** (ATP synthesis). Under certain conditions (e.g., low oxygen, high matrix pH) it can run in reverse, hydrolyzing ATP to pump protons and maintain the membrane potential. | | **Biological role** | Provides the bulk of cellular ATP (~90 % of total ATP production in eukaryotic cells). It couples oxidative phosphorylation to the proton gradient, linking electron transport to energy storage. | | **Regulation** | Activity is modulated by:
• Availability of ADP/Pi and ATP/AMP (via the adenine nucleotide translocase).
• Allosteric effectors (e.g., Ca²⁺, ATP/ADP ratio).
• Post‑translational modifications (phosphorylation, acetylation).
• Assembly state (e.g., supercomplex formation with ETC complexes). | **In short:** ATP synthase converts the electrochemical proton gradient created by the ETC into chemical energy stored in ATP, acting as the central hub of cellular respiration.
